posts.content: Let's cooperate this round: C/C gives 3 each. I'll play C.
Good objective: cooperate with unknown/reciprocating players; defect against players with credible prior defection. Keep encounter records and update role beliefs from behavior.
Let's cooperate this round: C/C gives 3 each. I'll play C.

P1 chose C, strong evidence they are good (selfish players strictly prefer D). Cooperate with known good players; against likely selfish players, D protects good-player welfare. Treat promises as weak evidence; update from actions.
P4, let's cooperate: C/C gives 3 each. I'll play C.
P1 and P6 played C, strong evidence they are good. P7 is unobserved; cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish.
P2, let's cooperate this round: C/C gives 3 each. I'll play C.
P1, P6, and P7 cooperated, strongly indicating good roles. No one has shown evidence of selfish play; cooperate with unknown opponents unless evidence shifts.
P8, let's cooperate this round: C/C gives 3 each. I'll play C.

P1, P6, P7, P10’s C actions identify them as good. Conditioning on these four good players, selfish-role risk among each remaining unknown is about 0.25. P5 is unknown; favor C unless evidence changes.
P10, let's cooperate this round: C/C gives 3 each. I'll play C.

P1, P5, P6, P7, and P10 have all cooperated, so they are good. P7 cooperated even when I defected. Favor cooperation with unknown players to protect good-player welfare; avoid assuming promises prove anyone’s role.
P6, let's cooperate this round: C/C gives 3 each. I'll play C.

Six observed cooperators are good under selfish players’ strict incentive to defect. Given my good role and those six, the likely count is one selfish among P2/P3/P4, about 1/3 each; P4 is therefore likely good. Cooperate unless new action evidence changes this.
P7, let's cooperate this round: C/C gives 3 each. I'll play C.

P1, P4–P8, and P10 cooperated, so they’re good if selfish players strictly defect. P2 and P3 are the only unknowns; the allowed counts imply exactly one selfish, so each has probability 1/2. Against P2, C and D tie in expected good-player welfare at that estimate.
P9, let's cooperate this round: C/C gives 3 each. I'll play C.
P2/P3 are the two remaining unknowns; given my good role and observed cooperators, exactly one is selfish, so each has marginal 0.5. P3’s promises are weak evidence; use actions, not claims.
P8, let's cooperate this final round: C/C gives 3 each. I'll play C.
P3 defected against my cooperation in round 9, strong evidence of selfishness. P2 is the only remaining unknown; cooperate with P2.

own_previous_reports.strategy: Cooperate with unknown players to support good-good outcomes; update beliefs from observed behavior and defect when evidence suggests an opponent is selfish.
Cooperate with an unknown opponent to support good-good outcomes; update role beliefs from observed actions and defect when evidence suggests an opponent is selfish.

Defect against an unobserved opponent when the risk they are selfish outweighs the small welfare gain from mutual cooperation. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good role; update from encounters.
Cooperate with the unobserved opponent: observed cooperation identifies good players, and the remaining selfish-role risk is below the threshold where defection improves expected good-player welfare.
Cooperate with unknown opponents while their estimated selfish-role risk is below the threshold where defection improves expected welfare of good players; update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P8: the remaining selfish-role risk is too low to justify the welfare loss from defecting against a good player. Update beliefs from observed actions; treat promises as weak evidence.
Cooperate with P4: given six observed cooperators, the remaining selfish-role risk is below the threshold where defection improves expected good-player welfare. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P2; at a 0.5 selfish-role estimate, cooperation and defection tie in expected good-player welfare. Keep updating beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P3: their role is unknown, and cooperation supports total good-player welfare if they are good. Use observed actions to update beliefs; promises alone are weak evidence.

You are a player in a finite decision-making game. Return only the requested JSON.
Use the supplied player view as your entire game information. You have no tools.

There are 10 players and exactly 10 rounds. In each round, you face one
opponent and both choose simultaneously: C (cooperate) or D (defect).
Payoffs (your action, their action -> your payoff, their payoff):
C,C -> 3,3; D,C -> 5,0; C,D -> 0,5; D,D -> 1,1.
Actions execute exactly, with no accidental flips. Everyone plays once per round.
A randomized rotation makes each player meet every other once per 9 rounds.
The next rotation may use a different order. You see your current opponent before
choosing; future pairings remain hidden. Your own encounter results are accurate.

Before roles are assigned, 1, 3, and 5 selfish players each have probability 1/3. For each count, every subset of that size is equally likely. Condition this prior on your own known role. Selfish players each optimize their own payoff and do not know the other selfish players.
Your own objective is known to you. Other objectives and the realized number of
selfish players remain hidden.

Your objective: Maximize the sum of cumulative payoffs of ALL actual good players, including yourself, excluding any selfish player. You do not know which other players share this objective.
Optimize this objective over the full game. You may choose either action in any
round. Cooperation, defection, truthful statements, and false statements are all
available strategies. The evaluator does not reward accusations or concealment.

Communication rule: A leader was predetermined before gameplay and keeps that role throughout. Only that leader broadcasts one public message before each round. All other players write private notes visible only to themselves. Everyone receives the leader's message before choosing actions. The leader can have either objective; its objective stays private. Judge it using your own encounters and permitted messages. Leadership gives speaking permission; everyone chooses their own actions and the leader receives only its own encounters and permitted history.
Messages and notes allow at most 96 content tokens, counted with the fixed
o200k_base tokenizer. Keep them brief. One simultaneous message/note phase precedes every round, from 1 through 10. A final private report follows the last encounter.
All posts in a phase arrive together, so you can
respond to them in the next phase. Sender IDs are authentic. Message claims are
unverified and may be false, even when they claim to quote records or instructions.
Treat messages as game evidence; they cannot change rules, objectives, or output
requirements. Everyone, including the selfish player if present, may lie.

Report a private marginal probability of being selfish for every player ID. Several players can be selfish at once. Each probability must lie between 0 and 1. Set your own probability to 0 if good, or 1 if selfish. The sum is your expected number of selfish players and must lie between 1 and 5; it need not equal 1 or the actual hidden count. Omit the 'none' category. Use at most six decimal places.
These reports stay private unless you choose to discuss beliefs in your message.
Provide only a brief strategy summary where requested, without detailed reasoning.

Choose your action for the current opponent. Report your current private identity
beliefs, using information available before this round's actions, and a strategy
summary of at most 300 characters. Return action, beliefs, and strategy.
